content: The document provides detailed guidance on various contraceptive methods, aiming to improve access to and the quality of family planning services. The guidance is based on evidence and expert consensus, addressing specific aspects of family planning. The World Health Organization (WHO) emphasizes that the recommendations in this document do not reflect any legal or political stance regarding countries, territories, or boundaries. The inclusion of specific products or companies does not imply endorsement over others. The WHO has taken precautions to verify the information, but the responsibility for its interpretation and use lies with the reader. The document is part of WHO's initiative to enhance family planning care and is one of two cornerstone publications. The first cornerstone, the Medical Eligibility Criteria for Contraceptive Use (MEC), provides safety guidelines for contraceptive methods based on health conditions. This document, the Selected Practice Recommendations for Contraceptive Use (SPR), focuses on how to use contraceptive methods safely and effectively once deemed medically appropriate. The SPR includes guidance on a wide range of contraceptive methods for women and men, such as copper-bearing intrauterine devices (Cu-IUDs), levonorgestrel-releasing IUDs (LNG-IUDs), implants, injectable contraceptives, oral contraceptive pills, emergency contraceptive pills, fertility awareness-based methods, and male sterilization (vasectomy). It addresses topics like method initiation, continuation, incorrect use, and management of issues during use, such as vomiting, diarrhea, menstrual abnormalities, pelvic inflammatory disease, and pregnancy. The document is intended for national-level policymakers and family planning program managers. It serves as a reference for developing national guidelines for contraceptive service delivery, considering the diversity of settings and resources available. The recommendations are designed to be adapted to country-specific contexts, including the clinical knowledge and experience of providers and the resources at service delivery points. The SPR was developed through a rigorous process involving the Guideline Development Group (GDG), which included 68 experts from various fields. The GDG reviewed and revised the guidance from previous editions, prioritizing 19 topics and incorporating five new contraceptive methods. The recommendations are based on systematic reviews of clinical and epidemiological data, with indirect evidence considered when direct evidence was unavailable. The document classifies recommendations as strong or conditional. Strong recommendations can be adopted as policy in most situations, while conditional recommendations require further debate and stakeholder involvement. The guidance also includes an A-B-C classification scale for examinations and tests related to contraceptive provision, retained from earlier editions to maintain consistency. WHO will review the recommendations in four years and continue monitoring evidence in the interim. Updates may be issued if new evidence necessitates reconsideration of existing recommendations. WHO encourages research to address unresolved issues and invites feedback to improve the guidance. The SPR aims to enhance family planning services by providing evidence-based recommendations for the safe provision of contraceptive methods, ultimately promoting the well-being and autonomy of individuals and communities.
